question.text: A 50-year-old woman with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) presents to your clinic with complaints of left eye pain and reduced vision. She notes that she was in her usual state of health until 3 days prior to presentation when she noticed some mild tenderness around her left eye, unrelieved by any pain relievers. This morning when she woke up she was unable to see out of her left eye and made an appointment to come see you. Other than SLE, her medical history is unremarkable. She has had no additional symptoms other than pain and vision loss. Her vital signs are all within normal limits. On exam, she has no vision in her left eye, but 20/30 visual acuity in her right eye. When you shine a light in her left eye there is no response. What response would you expect when you shine a light in her right eye?

options.B: Miosis of the right eye only
options.C: Miosis of the left eye only
options.F: I don't know or cannot answer

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's presentation of acute unilateral vision loss in the setting of SLE strongly suggests uveitis. The lack of response to light in the affected eye indicates a problem with the iris or the anterior chamber. Given the patient's SLE, the most likely diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis. In acute anterior uveitis, the affected eye typically shows a constricted pupil (miosis), while the unaffected eye usually maintains a normal pupil size. The patient's right eye is unaffected, so it would be expected to have a normal pupil size.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Acute anterior uveitis in SLE typically presents with miosis in the affected eye and a normal pupil in the unaffected eye.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Other possible causes of vision loss include optic neuritis, retinal detachment, and angle-closure glaucoma. However, the acute onset of pain and the lack of response to light in the affected eye are more consistent with uveitis. While optic neuritis can cause vision loss, it is less likely to present with acute pain and a non-reactive pupil. Retinal detachment typically presents with a visual field defect, not complete vision loss. Angle-closure glaucoma can cause vision loss, but it is usually associated with severe eye pain, headache, and nausea/vomiting, which are not mentioned in this case.
